Section 1

What this app is, and why it exists

The research asks whether the Harit Pathsala Eco-Score can be trusted. The notebook proves it on paper; this app lets someone find out by clicking.

The original calculator gives a student one number out of 100. The research found that number is sound in the middle of its range and silent at the ends — 9.19% of a simulated school scores exactly 0, with real footprints spanning 2.99 to 8.91 kg CO₂/day. Reading that in a paper is one thing. Dragging a slider and watching the score refuse to move is another.

So the app has one job: score the same student three ways at once — the original, and the two proposed replacements — and let you see where they agree and where the original stops responding. Everything else on the four pages exists to explain that comparison.

Who it is for A supervisor checking the research; a teacher deciding whether to trust the score; and the next student who picks this project up. It is not a replacement for the Harit Pathsala app itself — that app is untouched.

Section 2

Running it

Locally

pip install -r research/webapp/requirements.txt
streamlit run research/webapp/app.py

It opens on http://localhost:8501. Run the notebook first if you have not — the Findings page embeds the PNGs from research/figures/ and will show a warning box in place of any that is missing.

If streamlit is not a recognised command The package can be installed without its launcher being on your PATH. Use the module form instead, which always works: 
python3 -m streamlit run research/webapp/app.py

Deployed

The app is deployed on Streamlit Community Cloud from the public repository Jayed-Alam-Mansur/harit-pathsala-eco-score-research, main file webapp/app.py. Community Cloud watches the branch and rebuilds automatically on every push — a code change reboots the app in about a minute; a change to requirements.txt rebuilds the environment and takes a few minutes.

If visitors are asked to sign in That is the app's viewer setting, not the repository's. The repo is public, but a Community Cloud app can still require authentication. Open the app's Settings → Sharing and allow anyone with the link to view.

Section 3

How it works

Two Python files, one of which contains no interface code at all. That separation is the reason the app and the paper can never disagree.

eco_score_research.ipynbRuns the analysis, writes 14 figures and key_results.json
→
data/key_results.jsonEvery published and recomputed number, in one file
→
webapp/model.pyFormulas, constants, population generator — pure NumPy
→
webapp/app.pyFour pages of interface, no formulas of its own

model.py — the shared source of truth

This module holds the emission factors, the uncertainty percentages, the population specification, the published results, and the five functions that do the actual work. It imports only numpy and pandas — no Streamlit, no plotting, no file I/O at import time. That is deliberate: the notebook imports the very same module and asserts that its own definitions agree with it bit for bit, on every function and on the entire 10,000-student population. If the two ever drift apart, the notebook stops with an error rather than quietly publishing two different sets of numbers.

FunctionWhat it does
calculate_footprint(…)five answers → daily kg CO₂ and the five category contributions
eco_score(F)the original clamped min–max score
eco_score_percentile(F)Method A — boundaries at the population's 5th/95th percentile
eco_score_logistic(F)Method B — the recommended logistic curve
generate_population(…)a reproducible synthetic school as a DataFrame
analytical_score_sd(…)propagated emission-factor uncertainty for one student
monte_carlo_scores(…)the same uncertainty by simulation

app.py — interface only

Four pages behind a sidebar radio. Every expensive call is wrapped in @st.cache_data, so the 10,000-student population and the Monte Carlo draws are computed once and reused as you move sliders. The page also detects your Streamlit version and uses the modern width="stretch" layout argument where available, falling back to the older use_container_width — which is why it runs cleanly on both Streamlit 1.32 and 1.60 without a wall of deprecation warnings.

Section 4 · Page One

🏠 Calculator

The page that makes the argument. One student, scored three ways, updating on every input change.

The inputs, left column

How do you get to school?
walk, bicycle, bus, motorbike or car. Walking and cycling have an emission factor of exactly 0, so distance stops mattering for them.
One-way distance
0.5–20 km. The formula doubles it for the return trip — do not enter the round trip yourself.
Monthly electricity
10–300 kWh, from the NEA bill. Divided by 30 for a daily figure.
Has rooftop solar?
swaps the grid factor (0.23) for the solar lifecycle factor (0.04) — a large drop, which is why so few students have it and it matters so much when they do.
LPG cylinders per month
0.25–4. One Nepali cylinder is 14.2 kg. If a cylinder lasts two months, enter 0.5.
Daily household waste
the app's own three options: 0.3, 0.6 or 1.2 kg.
Monthly stationery spend
0–600 NPR. Included for completeness; it is the weakest input by a factor of 62.
The defaults are not arbitrary They are the worked example documented in docs/calculator-math.md: bus, 2 km, 90 kWh, 1 cylinder, medium waste, Rs 200. They produce 1.976 kg CO₂/day and an Eco-Score of 41. If you ever see anything else on a fresh load, something has broken.

The results, right column

Three score tiles. Original, Percentile, and Logistic ★. The first carries a delta against the worked example's 41, so you can see at a glance whether the student you built is better or worse than the documented one. Below them, the same footprint as daily, monthly and yearly totals — the absolute numbers that keep their meaning when the score does not.

Category breakdown. A horizontal bar per category in the five fixed colours used by every figure in the research: transport blue, electricity orange, cooking yellow, waste green, stationery mauve.

The scoring curves. All three functions over 0–5 kg CO₂/day, with the original's two dead zones shaded grey, a dashed red line at the current footprint, and a dot where the student lands on each curve. This single chart is the research in one picture.

The context box

Below the charts, one of three messages depending on where the student sits:

ZoneWhat it says
F < 0.5Green. The original gives 100 but cannot distinguish this student from any other very low emitter; the logistic can.
0.5 ≤ F ≤ 3.0Blue. The responsive zone — all three methods broadly agree, because the original is working as intended.
F > 3.0Red. The dead zone. The original reports 0 while the logistic still reports a moving score.

“How reliable is this score?”

The expander at the bottom propagates emission-factor uncertainty for this student, showing the 95% range, a 1,000-draw Monte Carlo histogram, and the analytical and simulated standard deviations side by side. For the default student those are ±5.92 and ±5.99 points — agreeing to 1.29%. If more than half a percent of the draws hit a clamp, an extra warning appears, because near a boundary the score is not merely uncertain but systematically distorted.

The demonstration worth doing live

Set transport to Car and distance to 7 km, then drag the distance down one step at a time:

DistanceFootprintOriginalLogistic ★
7 km4.57 kg/day02
6 km4.19 kg/day03
5 km3.81 kg/day06
4 km3.43 kg/day011
3 km3.05 kg/day018
Stay inside 7 → 3 km Beyond about 8 km the logistic also rounds to 0 on the tile and the contrast disappears; below about 2.6 km the original starts responding again. This window is the only place the point is visible.

Section 5 · Page Two

📊 Research Findings

The five findings, each as an expandable section carrying the notebook's own figure — nothing is redrawn by hand for the app.

Four tiles across the top: mean Eco-Score 31.9, floor saturation 9.19%, score uncertainty ±5.92 points, and the dead zone after the fix.

FindingWhat it shows
1 — Cooking and electricity control the score The five sensitivities as a bar chart, and the 62× ratio between cooking (-2.859) and stationery (-0.046).
2 — A score of 41 could mean 29 to 53 Analytical against Monte Carlo standard deviation, their 1.29% agreement, and the 10,000-draw histogram.
3 — 9.19% of students are silenced The saturation histogram, the 2.99–8.91 kg/day spread, and the household baseline of 2.048 kg/day that explains why the floor fills up.
4 — The formula is perfect, the clamp is broken R² across everyone against R² = 0.9997 once the floored students are removed.
5 — Two better alternatives The three curves overlaid, the comparison table, and the recommendation with its trade-off stated.

Section 6 · Page Three

🎓 Understanding the Math

For the reader who wants to know why, not just what. Two of the four sections are interactive.

Where the formula came from

Each emission factor's physical derivation, including the two worth showing on a board: an LPG cylinder as 14.2 × 1.51 = 21.442 kg CO₂, and the bus factor as 2.68 ÷ (4 × 40) = 0.016 kg CO₂ per passenger-kilometre.

What is sensitivity analysis?

Partial derivatives in plain English, then the key result — ∂S/∂xᵢ = −40 θᵢ inside the responsive region and exactly 0 outside it. Interactive: pick a category and sweep it from 0% to 200% of the worked example, and watch the score curve flatten the moment it leaves the responsive band.

What is Monte Carlo simulation?

Three paragraphs answering the question directly: randomness as a computational trick in algorithms (Miller–Rabin, randomised QuickSort) versus randomness as a property of the physical world here. Interactive: a slider for the number of simulations, from 100 to 10,000, plotting the estimated standard deviation converging onto the analytical 5.92 — error shrinking like 1/√N, which is exactly why 10,000 is the sensible stopping point.

Why the logistic?

What k = 1.7202 and F₀ = 2.1883 mean in words, a slider to move a student's footprint along all three curves at once, and the entropy comparison as a bar chart against the theoretical maximum of ln(20) = 2.996 nats.

Section 7 · Page Four

📁 About This Project

The narrative, the limitations, and a tool for trying the research on a class of your own.

The left column tells the story in four parts — where it started, what was studied and why, what was found, what is recommended — and states the three limitations plainly rather than burying them: the population is simulated rather than surveyed, the logistic scale is population-relative, and the emission factors were assumed to vary independently.

The class simulator

Choose a class size (10–200) and a random seed, and the app generates that many students from the same distributions used in the research, scores them all three ways, and reports mean, standard deviation, percentage at the floor and percentage at the ceiling for each method, with three histograms side by side. The class can be downloaded as CSV.

Why this matters more than it looks It lets a teacher discover the floor problem on a class of 40 rather than being told about it on a population of 10,000 — and changing the seed shows how much the floor percentage varies between classes, which is a more honest picture than a single headline number.

There is also a download button for key_results.json, so anyone reading the app can take the underlying numbers away and check them.

Section 8

Where every number on screen comes from

No figure displayed by the app is typed into the app.

The notebook computes everything and writes data/key_results.json. That file carries several blocks:

BlockContents
key_resultsthe published, canonical numbers quoted in the paper and shown by the app
recomputedthe same quantities as recalculated by the latest notebook run
validationthe percentage deviation between the two, per key
emission_factors, uncertainty, population_specthe model's inputs
worked_example, population_summary, metathe verification case, distribution summary and run metadata

The app reads the published block from model.KEY_RESULTS, so the interface, the paper and the slide deck all quote one consistent set.

One inconsistency you may notice, and it is deliberate The app's “Dead Zone Reduced” tile reads 0.25% (the published value), while the narrative document and the slide deck use 0.3% (the recomputed value) in the calibration chapter. The gap is 0.05 percentage points — about five students in ten thousand — and both are recorded in key_results.json. The same applies to R² across the full population: published 0.8538, recomputed 0.8639. The notebook prints the full deviation table in its Section 6, and docs/research_notes.md §2.1 explains why five of the thirty published values cannot be reproduced to the last digit.

Section 9

Changing it

Replace the synthetic population with real data

This is the change that matters most. Run the survey specified in data/survey_template.md — seven questions, three minutes, no personal data, wording given in English and Nepali. Export a CSV whose columns match the generator's output exactly:

transport_mode, distance_km, electricity_kwh, has_solar,
lpg_cylinders, waste_kg_day, stationery_npr

Then swap generate_population() for a read_csv in the notebook's Section 4 and re-run. The percentile boundaries, the logistic k and F₀, and the floor percentage all recompute from real answers. At least 100 responses are needed before a median is stable enough to anchor a scoring scale.

Change an emission factor or an uncertainty

Edit the dictionary in model.py — but the notebook will then fail its Section 0 verification, because the worked example no longer matches the documented one. That failure is the feature. Update the documented example deliberately, or revert.

Change the scoring boundaries

The defaults of eco_score_percentile and eco_score_logistic live in model.py. Change them in the notebook too, or the cross-check in Section 0 will fail — again, by design.

Add a page

Add its label to the sidebar radio list and a matching elif page == … branch. Keep formulas out of app.py: if a new page needs maths, it belongs in model.py where the notebook can verify it.

Section 10

Troubleshooting

SymptomCause and fix
command not found: streamlit The launcher is not on PATH. Use python3 -m streamlit run ….
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'model' Should not happen — app.py adds its own directory to sys.path at import. If you copied app.py elsewhere, take model.py with it.
“Figure not found” boxes on the Findings page research/figures/ is empty. Run the notebook once; it writes all 14 figures.
Port already in use Another app is on 8501. Pass --server.port 8610 or whichever port is free.
The app looks dark, not light The theme lives in .streamlit/config.toml at the repository root and is read relative to the working directory. Launch from that directory, or pass --theme.base light.
Deployed app asks visitors to log in App-level sharing setting, separate from repository visibility. Change it in the app's Settings → Sharing.
Deployed app has not picked up a change Community Cloud rebuilds on push to the tracked branch. Confirm the commit is on main; a dependency change takes minutes rather than seconds.
